Tirade

/tuh-RAYD/ — stress on second syllable, rhymes with wade · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A tirade is a long, angry speech of criticism or complaint.

The manager launched into a tirade after discovering the shipment had been delayed again.

Worked Example

When the restaurant failed to get her order right for the third time, the frustrated customer launched into a fierce tirade, venting months of disappointment and anger about their service.

Tirade captures not just anger but a long, flowing outpouring of criticism — it's a speech, not just a moment of irritation. Just 'complaint' or 'anger' would miss the sense of words tumbling out in a torrent of blame and frustration.

How Tirade Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

complaint

complaint: a milder statement that something is unsatisfactory

rant

rant: loud, rambling angry talk, less focused

harangue

harangue: a lengthy, aggressive lecture scolding its listeners

Antonyms

praise

praise: warm approving words instead of criticism

commendation

commendation: formal spoken or written praise given officially

How Strong Is It? — complaint → outburst → rant → tirade

complaint vs. tirade

complaint vs. tirade: A complaint is far weaker than a tirade — it briefly points out a problem, while a tirade unleashes a long, furious speech about it.

outburst vs. tirade

outburst vs. tirade: An outburst is stronger than a complaint but still weaker than a tirade, because it is a short flash of anger rather than a tirade's extended, driving attack.

rant vs. tirade

rant vs. tirade: A rant comes close to a tirade in heat, but a tirade is stronger — more sustained, more bitter, and more sharply aimed at its target.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — tirade

Root — tirade: a long angry speech or volley of words (French)

Put it together

Put it together: Tirade comes into English as a single unit from French tirer, 'to draw, pull, or shoot' — literally something 'shot forth': a long volley of angry words fired at someone. There is no prefix or suffix to peel off here; the whole word, borrowed straight from French, carries the meaning of a long, angry speech of criticism or complaint.

Use the root in a new word: retire

Use the root in a new word: retire: When the exhausted general decided to retire from the battlefield, he literally drew himself back — re- (back) + tirer (to draw) — pulling his troops away from the fight.

Word Choice

formal / literary

Tirade is the word when anger builds into a speech — a long, forceful outpouring of criticism or blame. It's more dramatic than 'complaint' and more structured than 'rant.' Reach for it when you want to show that anger has turned into words, rolling out like a torrent.
